It was a Sunday afternoon, and I had been in the country for some weeks now with the family of my former playmates. We were all walking through the park; we came upon the big house which used to be called the “Castle.” It stood out like a gigantic toy castle, quite uncompleted, but quite beautiful. A little stream flowed past it; its waters ran down the hillside into the garden pond, over which there was a small bridge leading to a gate. The gateway itself was an open arch, painted white, but without any other decoration than this: behind the arch there grew a single tree, bare of leaves. In front of the arch the wall continued high up to a great stone pillar. At the foot of this pillar there grew a second tree—another bare tree—but one with long green branches, and these were covered with the flowers of spring. They looked exactly like a miniature orchard. But the most remarkable thing in that scene is the fact that nothing could be more perfect, and yet everything was missing.

The idea of a finished picture struck me then, and has always remained with me ever since. I have never seen anything more like the conception of a work that shall never be done than that unfinished building. I can hear the children playing around it, or perhaps the old man who lived in it himself singing songs. And even if no human voice should ever come out of that house, I feel sure that music would sing inside, and that voices of men and angels would rise from every corner, while all sorts of things would happen in those silent halls.
